title: Ethiopian Roasted Sweet Potato
localName: ስኳር ድንች ቆሎ — Suqar Dinich Qolo
community: Ethiopian street vendors — the most affordable sweet snack
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Ember-Roasted Sweet Potato — whole sweet potatoes placed directly in glowing charcoal embers and roasted until the skin chars and the inside becomes sweet, caramelised, and fluffy. The most affordable street snack in Ethiopia — sold by vendors whose braziers glow at every street corner.
longDesc: Ember-roasted sweet potato is the sweet snack that no Ethiopian street corner is without — the blackened whole sweet potatoes piled in large baskets beside charcoal braziers, sold by vendors who peel them to order. The natural sweetness is intensified by the charcoal heat.
ingredients: 4 medium orange-fleshed sweet potatoes — scrubbed but unpeeled
equipment: Charcoal brazier or open fire with glowing embers
steps: Place whole sweet potatoes directly into the glowing charcoal embers.
The skin should be completely charred and black.
Test with a skewer — no resistance means done.
The inside should be fluffy, sweet, and orange.
Serve with a pinch of salt.
chefTips: The skin must be completely charred — this is not burning, this is the cooking method.
The interior should be almost molten-sweet — this is the goal.
commonMistakes: Not leaving long enough — undercooked sweet potato is starchy.
cookingScience: Ember roasting creates a thermal gradient — the exterior chars at 400°C+ while the interior slowly rises to about 100°C. At 100°C, the sweet potato's amylase enzymes (still active below 80°C during the slow heat-up) convert starch to maltose and glucose — a process called 'enzyme-driven gelatinisation' that produces the characteristic extreme sweetness of properly roasted sweet potato.
sustainabilityTips: Sweet potatoes require minimal water to grow — among the most sustainable crops available.
servedWith: With a pinch of mitmita for heat
culturalNote: Ember-roasted sweet potato is the most democratic street food in Ethiopia — at one birr per potato, it is affordable for everyone. The vendor's brazier on a cold highland evening, the stack of blackened sweet potatoes, and the warmth of holding one while peeling it — this is Ethiopian street food at its most elemental.
